title: P-Values, Power and False Discoveries
description: What a significant result does and does not tell you, and why low power matters

concepts.title: What a P-Value Actually Says
concepts.contentHtml:
Every lesson in this topic turns on one number. A p-value is the probability of getting data at least as extreme as yours if a stated null hypothesis (usually "no effect") and every other assumption of the statistical model were true. Ronald Fisher developed the idea in the 1920s while studying crop variance in Hertfordshire, and he offered it as a way to stop researchers declaring truth from patterns in noise.1 By convention, a p-value below 0.05 counts as "statistically significant".

Notice the direction of the conditional. A p-value is the probability of the data given the null, not the probability of the null given the data. The two can differ as much as the chance that a pope is Catholic differs from the chance that a Catholic is the pope. So p = 0.03 does not mean a 3% chance that the result is a fluke, and it certainly does not mean a 97% chance that your hypothesis is true.

These misreadings became so widespread that in March 2016 the American Statistical Association's board issued a statement on p-values for the first time.2 Its six principles include these:

  • P-values can indicate how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model.
  • They do not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true, or the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone.
  • Scientific conclusions should not rest only on whether a p-value passes a specific threshold.
  • A p-value does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result.

Ron Wasserstein, the association's executive director, put it bluntly: the p-value was never intended to be a substitute for scientific reasoning.3 Jessica Utts, then its president, added that p had become a gatekeeper for publication in some fields. Both ideas return in lesson 2. For now, hold on to the narrow truth: a p-value describes one dataset under one model, and says nothing about whether the analysis was chosen before or after the data were seen.

concepts.title: Power: The Forgotten Half of the Test
concepts.contentHtml:
A significance test can go wrong in two ways. A Type I error (false positive) declares an effect that is not there, and psychology caps its rate at α = 0.05. A Type II error (false negative) misses an effect that is real; its probability is β. Power, 1 − β, is the chance that a study detects an effect of a given size if it exists. It rises with the true effect size, the sample size and α. Effects of d = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8, where d is the difference between groups in standard deviations, are traditionally called small, medium and large.

Power is easy to neglect because you never see the studies that missed. Take a medium effect, d = 0.5, and a two-group experiment with 20 people per group: power is only about a third. To reach 80% power you need about 64 per group. In 1962 Jacob Cohen surveyed the Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology and found a median power of 0.46 for medium effects, roughly a coin toss. In 2017 Denes Szucs and John Ioannidis analysed 26,841 statistical records from 3,801 recent cognitive neuroscience and psychology papers. Median power to detect small, medium and large effects was 0.12, 0.44 and 0.73, reflecting no improvement through the past half-century, because sample sizes had stayed small.1

Low power does more than waste effort. When a small study does reach significance, it has usually caught a lucky overestimate, because only large observed effects clear the bar. This winner's curse inflates published effects in underpowered fields. Szucs and Ioannidis found a median reported effect size of d = 0.93 for significant results but 0.24 for non-significant ones.2 Katherine Button and colleagues made the same case for neuroscience in 2013: the consequences of low power include overestimates of effect size and low reproducibility.3 Keep that in mind, because the replication projects in lesson 4 found exactly this pattern: real effects, but smaller than first reported.

concepts.title: Why Most Published Findings Could Be False
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2005 John Ioannidis published an essay in PLoS Medicine with a deliberately provocative title, "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False". His case is arithmetic, not accusation. Whether a significant result is true depends on the study's power, the α level, and the pre-study odds R that the tested relationship is real at all. The positive predictive value (PPV), the share of significant findings that are true, follows from Bayes' rule, shown below.

Work an example. Suppose a field tests one true hypothesis for every ten false ones, so R = 0.1. With 80% power, PPV = 0.08 / (0.08 + 0.05), about 62%. Cut power to 35%, nearer what surveys of psychology have found, and PPV = 0.035 / 0.085, about 41%. Most significant results would then be false, with nobody cheating at all. Add bias, meaning analyses nudged towards significance, and it falls further.

Ioannidis drew out corollaries. In his framework, a research finding is less likely to be true when the studies conducted in a field are smaller, when effect sizes are smaller,1 when more relationships are tested with less preselection, when there is greater flexibility in designs, definitions, outcomes and analyses, when financial and other interests are stronger, and when more teams chase statistical significance in a field. Read that list against social psychology around 2010, with its small samples, subtle manipulations, many outcome measures and fierce competition for striking results, and the coming crisis looks less like bad luck than a forecast.

R is rarely known, so the numbers are illustrations rather than measurements. The lasting lesson is that a p-value alone cannot tell you how much to believe a result: you also need the plausibility of the hypothesis, the power of the study and the analyst's freedom. Szucs and Ioannidis estimated in 2017 that, assuming a realistic range of prior probabilities, the false report probability for the cognitive neuroscience and psychology literature is likely to exceed 50%.2

title: P-Hacking and the Garden of Forking Paths
description: How flexible analysis and selective publishing turn noise into significance

concepts.title: Researcher Degrees of Freedom
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2011 Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn reported in Psychological Science that music can make you younger. They asked 20 University of Pennsylvania undergraduates to listen to either "When I'm Sixty-Four" by The Beatles or a control track, "Kalimba". Controlling for each participant's father's age, those who heard The Beatles were, according to their birth dates, nearly a year and a half younger:1 adjusted means of 20.1 versus 21.5 years, p = .040.

The authors did not believe a word of it. They had run the study to show how standard practice manufactures findings, and they then gave the full account. They had tested 34 students, played a third song ("Hot Potato" by the Wiggles), analysed the data after every session of about 10 participants with no fixed stopping point, and collected a long list of other measures, from how old participants felt to their mother's age. Without the father's-age control, the difference was not significant (p = .33). Every choice was the kind researchers made routinely; together they produced an impossible result.

These choices are researcher degrees of freedom: the many small, defensible decisions made after the data start arriving. In simulations of 15,000 samples, the authors showed how quickly they compound:

  • Optional stopping: test after 20 participants, add 10 more if p is not yet below .05. This alone raises the false-positive rate by about 50%.2
  • Flexible outcomes: measure two dependent variables, report whichever works.
  • Covariates: control for gender, or not.
  • Dropping conditions: run three conditions, report two.

Used together, these freedoms gave a false-positive rate of about 61%:3 a researcher with the best intentions was more likely than not to find evidence for a false hypothesis. The proposed fix was disclosure, with six requirements for authors (such as deciding the sample size in advance and listing every variable) and four guidelines for reviewers.

concepts.title: The Garden of Forking Paths
concepts.contentHtml:
The word p-hacking suggests a researcher running test after test until one comes up significant. In 2014 Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken argued in American Scientist that the deeper problem needs no such fishing. A p-value is defined by what would have happened across other possible datasets, so it is valid only if the same analysis would have been run whatever the data looked like. If the choice of test depends on the data, even a single test is compromised.1 They called this the garden of forking paths.

Their main example came from Psychological Science in 2013, where Alec Beall and Jessica Tracy reported that women at peak fertility were three times more likely to wear red or pink shirts.2 Beall and Tracy said they had set out to test one specific hypothesis, and Gelman and Loken took them at their word. But the analysis still turned on choices: how strictly to set the age criteria for the women included, which hues counted as shades of red, the exact window of days counted as high conception risk, which interactions to examine, and whether to combine or contrast groups. None of this was preregistered.

The same journal that year published a study by Kristina Durante and colleagues claiming that ovulation made single women more liberal and married women more conservative, a swing of about 20 percentage points in vote intention.3 Gelman and Loken found that implausible, given how rarely people change their vote intentions during presidential campaigns. The two papers drew on similar stories and methods but used different exclusion rules and different days for comparison; one reported a main effect, the other a difference between single and married women. Each found significance in the comparison it focused on.

The uncomfortable lesson is that this applies to honest researchers using scientific common sense. The mistake is to treat significance on the path you happened to take as strong evidence for your hypothesis, when other data would have led you down a different path to a different significant result. The cure is commitment in advance, which preregistration (lesson 6) supplies.

concepts.title: The File Drawer and How to Detect It
concepts.contentHtml:
Flexible analysis inflates false positives within a study. Publication bias does it across studies. If journals mostly print significant results, the published record becomes a biased sample of what was actually found, while null results go into what researchers call the file drawer. Jessica Utts, president of the American Statistical Association in 2016, described research with statistically significant outcomes as much more likely to get published, while other work that might be just as important is never seen in print.1

How common were the questionable practices behind the bias? In 2012 Leslie John, George Loewenstein and Drazen Prelec surveyed over 2,000 psychologists, using an anonymous format with incentives for honest answers.2 The share who admitted to questionable research practices was surprisingly high, enough for the authors to suggest that some of these practices may constitute the prevailing research norm.3 Coverage of the Simmons paper cited a survey in which about seven in ten psychologists admitted making interim decisions about when to stop collecting data.4

Bias leaves fingerprints, and statisticians built tools to find them. In 2014 Simonsohn, Nelson and Simmons introduced p-curve, the distribution of statistically significant p-values across a set of studies. The logic runs like this:

  • If the null is true, p-values are uniformly distributed, so significant ones are spread evenly between 0 and .05.
  • If an effect is real and studies have reasonable power, very small p-values such as .01 outnumber ones just under the line, such as .04, giving a right-skewed curve.
  • If a literature has been p-hacked towards .05, results pile up just below the threshold.

Only right-skewed p-curves are diagnostic of evidential value.5 P-curve cannot tell you which individual study is wrong, but it can tell you whether a body of findings could be explained by selective reporting alone, which is exactly the question a reader of a biased literature needs answered.

title: 2011: Precognition, Priming and Fraud
description: Bem's psi paper, failed priming replications and the Stapel scandal force a reckoning

concepts.title: Feeling the Future
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2011 the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, one of the most prestigious journals in the field, published "Feeling the Future" by Daryl Bem, an emeritus professor of social psychology at Cornell University. It reported 9 experiments, involving more than 1,000 participants, that tested for1 precognition, the anomalous influence of future events on present responses. Bem's method was to "time-reverse" well-established psychological effects so that people responded before the supposedly causal stimulus occurred.

In one test of retroactive facilitation of recall, participants saw 48 words, took a surprise memory test, and only afterwards practised a random 24 of them. They recalled more of the words they were about to practise, as if revising after an exam improved the mark. In his first experiment, 100 students tried to anticipate whether a picture would appear on the left or the right; Bem found a significant result for erotic pictures but not for non-erotic ones. Across all 9 experiments the mean effect size was d = 0.22, and all but one of the experiments yielded statistically significant results.2

This was not a fringe outlet. The paper passed peer review at a top journal using the field's ordinary toolkit: randomised designs, significance tests and several studies converging on one conclusion. That was precisely the problem. Either precognition was real, or the ordinary toolkit could manufacture strong-looking evidence for something almost every scientist thought impossible.

Bem encouraged replication and put his software online. Stuart Ritchie, Richard Wiseman and Christopher French each repeated the recall experiment with 50 participants. All three preregistered attempts failed (combined n = 150, combined p = .83).3 When they submitted the work to the journal that had published Bem, they were told that it did not publish replications.4 The paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012, and the refusal became a symbol of a system that rewarded surprising claims and had no room for checking them.

concepts.title: Why Psi Put the Methods on Trial
concepts.contentHtml:
The sharpest reply came in the same journal in 2011. The psychometrician E. J. Wagenmakers and colleagues argued that Bem's analysis was partly exploratory and that his one-sided p-values overstated the evidence. Reanalysing the data with a default Bayesian t-test, they found the evidence for psi weak to nonexistent.1 Their real target was the discipline: Bem's p-values did not indicate evidence for precognition but showed that experimental psychologists needed to change the way they ran experiments and analysed data.

The Bayesian argument is worth unpacking. A p-value asks how surprising the data are if the null is true. A Bayes factor asks how much better one hypothesis predicts the data than another. The two can disagree sharply: a p just under .05 may correspond to data that barely favour the alternative, especially in large samples. And for a claim as implausible as precognition the prior odds should be tiny, so even a respectable Bayes factor leaves the posterior probability close to zero. This is Ioannidis's pre-study odds from lesson 1, applied to a single hypothesis.

Gelman and Loken added a forking-paths diagnosis. Bem, writing with the statisticians Jessica Utts and Wesley Johnson, insisted that his hypotheses came from earlier presentiment experiments and that no data exploration required adjustment. Gelman and Loken accepted the account of his motives but argued that each scientific hypothesis corresponded to many statistical ones. Had participants done significantly worse on erotic pictures, that too would have fitted the theory, since anomalous arousal might interfere with precognition. As they put it, the problem lay in the one-to-many mapping from scientific to statistical hypotheses.2

That is why Bem mattered more than any single fraud. Nobody needed to accuse him of misconduct. If the field's ordinary rules let precognition through, they would let other false findings through too, and nobody could say how many. Gelman and Loken called the case an example of how investigators can use well-accepted research practices to find statistical significance anywhere.3

concepts.title: Priming, Fraud and Kahneman's Warning
concepts.contentHtml:
Two more shocks landed alongside Bem. The first hit social priming, the idea that subtle cues unconsciously steer behaviour. Its icon was a 1996 study by John Bargh and colleagues in which participants unwittingly exposed to the stereotype of old age walked more slowly as they left the laboratory. In 2012 Stéphane Doyen and colleagues reported a replication with 120 Belgian students, timed automatically by two infrared sensors hidden in the hallway. They found no priming. In a second experiment they told half the experimenters that primed participants would walk slower: a walking-speed effect then appeared, but only when experimenters believed participants would walk slower.1

The second shock was fraud. Diederik Stapel, a prominent social psychologist at Tilburg University, admitted in 2011 to faking data. The final report of three investigating committees, presented on 28 November 2012, found that he had committed scientific fraud in no less than 55 publications, the earliest confirmed one dating from 2004.2 None of his co-authors or PhD students had been directly involved. The committees blamed a culture of poor science in which criticism had failed and his work had been received uncritically.

In 2012 Daniel Kahneman, the Nobel prize-winning psychologist at Princeton, sent an open email to researchers who work on social priming. He counted himself a general believer in priming effects, but he warned of a train wreck looming for the field,3 and told them it was now the poster child for doubts about the integrity of psychological research. His remedy was a daisy chain of replications: each lab would repeat a priming effect demonstrated by its neighbour, supervised by someone from the replicated lab,4 with every detail of the methods recorded, a commitment to publish made in advance and all data open.

Nearly every reform in this topic is foreshadowed in that email: direct replication, advance commitment, open data and many labs working together. Fraud was the scandal, but the deeper worry was that honest, standard work might be failing too.

title: Replication at Scale
description: The Reproducibility Project, Many Labs and the fight over what a failed replication means

concepts.title: One Hundred Studies, Repeated
concepts.contentHtml:
The most cited answer to "how bad is it?" came from the Reproducibility Project: Psychology. It was launched in 2011 by the Center for Open Science, a US non-profit, in the wake of the fraud scandals in psychology.1 One hundred studies were chosen from 2008 issues of three leading psychology journals, and about 350 scientists took part. The replications used high-powered designs and original materials when available, and the original authors were consulted along the way.

The results, published in Science on 28 August 2015, were sobering:

  • 97% of the original studies had statistically significant results; only 36% of the replications did.
  • Replication effects were half the magnitude of the original effects.2
  • 47% of original effect sizes fell inside the 95% confidence interval of the replication effect size.
  • 39% of effects were subjectively rated as having replicated.

Replication rates were particularly low in social psychology compared with cognitive psychology.3 And the best guide to success was not who ran the replication but the original evidence itself: replication success was better predicted by the strength of original evidence than by characteristics of the original and replication teams.4 That is what lesson 1's arithmetic predicts, since weak evidence is where false positives hide.

Be careful about what the project did not show. It did not prove that 64% of psychology is false. A single replication can miss a real effect, especially one that is real but smaller than first reported, and a replication can differ from the original in ways that matter. Assuming no bias in the original results, combining original and replication data left 68% of effects statistically significant. What the project measured was narrower and still important: how often a careful, independent team following the same recipe could obtain a published significant result again. By most of its measures, the answer was well under half the time.

concepts.title: Many Labs: One Protocol, Dozens of Sites
concepts.contentHtml:
The Reproducibility Project ran each replication once, in one place. The Many Labs projects, organised by Richard Klein, Michelangelo Vianello, Brian Nosek and many colleagues, ran each effect in many places at once using one shared protocol. That design separates two questions: does the effect exist at all, and does its size depend on the sample and setting?

Many Labs 1, published in 2014, tested the replicability of 13 classic and contemporary effects across 36 independent samples totalling 6,344 participants.1 Ten effects replicated consistently. One, imagined contact reducing prejudice, showed weak support. Two did not replicate: flag priming influencing conservatism and currency priming influencing system justification.2 Whether data were collected in the lab or online, or in the US or elsewhere, by and large made no difference.

Many Labs 2, published in 2018, was bigger and harder. It ran preregistered replications of 28 classic and contemporary findings, with protocols peer reviewed in advance. Each protocol was given to roughly half of 125 samples, 15,305 participants in all, from 36 countries and territories. With the conventional p < .05, 15 of the 28 (54%) replicated in the original direction. The median effect size fell from d = 0.60 in the original studies to 0.15 in the replications,3 and 9 replications (32%) pointed in the opposite direction from the original finding.

Just as important was what did not vary. Very little heterogeneity was attributable to task order, to lab versus online administration, or to exploratory comparisons between WEIRD (Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic) and less WEIRD cultures. Variability in observed effect sizes was more attributable to the effect being studied than the sample or setting in which it was studied.4 Roughly speaking, effects that worked tended to work widely, and effects that failed tended to fail everywhere.

concepts.title: What Does a Failed Replication Mean?
concepts.contentHtml:
A failed replication is evidence, not a verdict, and the field fought hard over how to read the Reproducibility Project. In 2016 Daniel Gilbert, Gary King, Stephen Pettigrew and Timothy Wilson argued in Science that the project contained three statistical errors and provided no support for its pessimistic conclusion. Indeed, they wrote, the data were consistent with the opposite conclusion: that the reproducibility of psychological science is quite high.1 Defenders of individual findings often appealed to hidden moderators, unnoticed differences of population, procedure or context that might make a true effect vanish in a new lab.

The project team replied that this very optimistic assessment rested on statistical misconceptions and on causal inferences from selectively interpreted, correlational data. Their own summary was measured: both optimistic and pessimistic conclusions about reproducibility were possible from these data, and neither was yet warranted.2 That remains a fair reading of a single project in which each study was repeated once.

Two later results undercut the hidden-moderator defence. Many Labs 2 found little variation across 36 countries and territories. And in 2018 Colin Camerer and colleagues replicated 21 systematically selected social-science experiments published in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015, with samples on average about five times larger than the originals and analysis plans reviewed by the original authors and preregistered. Thirteen (62%) showed a significant effect in the original direction, at on average about 50% of the original effect size.3

Most telling of all, the team had gathered researchers' beliefs about which studies would replicate, and those peer beliefs were strongly related to the results. The community could predict which findings would fail, so the failures were not the result of chance alone.4 Something about the original evidence, perhaps its implausibility, its small samples or its borderline p-values, already signalled weakness to experienced readers.

title: Effects That Faded, Effects That Held
description: Ego depletion, power posing and facial feedback under large preregistered tests

concepts.title: Ego Depletion: Willpower as a Fuel Tank
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1998 Roy Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Mark Muraven and Dianne Tice proposed that self-control draws on a limited inner resource that runs down with use, a state they called ego depletion. Their first experiment became a textbook classic. Participants arrived hungry, having eaten nothing for at least three hours, to a room filled with the smell of chocolate chip cookies baked on the spot. Some were told to eat only radishes; others could eat the cookies and chocolates; a control group had no food. All then tried unsolvable puzzles. People who forced themselves to eat radishes instead of tempting chocolates quit faster:1 after about 8 minutes on average, against about 19 for the chocolate group and 21 for the controls.

A multitude of studies followed, and in 2010 a meta-analysis of 83 studies by Hagger and colleagues found a significant effect of depletion on self-control performance. Later meta-analyses questioned the size and even the existence of the effect and found signs of bias. So in 2016 Hagger led a Registered Replication Report: 23 laboratories and 2,141 participants following one standardised sequential-task protocol.2 The pooled effect was d = 0.04, with a 95% confidence interval from −0.07 to 0.15 that included zero.3

Defenders, including Baumeister and his frequent co-author Kathleen Vohs, argued that the protocol was a poor test of the theory. In 2021 Vohs and colleagues ran their own preregistered test across 36 laboratories and 3,531 participants, using two procedures common in the published depletion literature. The confirmatory result was d = 0.06, not significant,4 and Bayesian analyses found the data four times more likely under the null than under an informed alternative. Exploratory analyses hinted at a larger effect among participants who reported more fatigue.

Whether some form of depletion exists is still argued. But the strong claim, that a few minutes of resisting cookies reliably drains a general willpower tank, has not survived large preregistered tests, including one led by its own advocates.

concepts.title: Power Poses and Pens in Mouths
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and A. J. Yap reported that adopting expansive "high-power" postures caused physiological change: high-power posers experienced elevations in testosterone, decreases in cortisol, and increased feelings of power and tolerance for risk. They concluded that a person can, by assuming two simple 1-minute poses, embody power and instantly become more powerful. Power posing spread far beyond the laboratory as self-help advice.

In 2015 Eva Ranehill and colleagues at the University of Zurich tested 102 men and 98 women with the same kind of risk task.1 They found no effect on hormones or on risk-taking, although participants did report feeling more powerful. Carney then posted a statement on her faculty website: "I do not believe that 'power pose' effects are real.2" She itemised the original study's weaknesses: a final sample of just 42, subjects run in chunks with the effect checked along the way, a likelihood-ratio p of .05 reported in place of a Pearson chi-square p of .052, and self-report items chosen because they "worked". Cuddy has continued to defend a narrower claim about feelings of power, and a 2018 p-curve analysis by her team reported clear evidential value for postural-feedback effects.

The facial feedback hypothesis shows how untidy the truth can be. In a 1988 study by Strack, Martin and Stepper, people rated cartoons while holding a pen either in their teeth, which forces a smile, or in their lips, which forces a pout. The "smilers" found the cartoons funnier, by 0.82 units on a 10-point scale. A 2016 Registered Replication Report of 17 direct replications found a difference of 0.03 units.3 Yet in 2022 the Many Smiles Collaboration, a global adversarial collaboration whose authors included Strack, tested 3,878 people in 19 countries. Facial mimicry and voluntary smiling could both amplify and initiate feelings of happiness;4 only the unobtrusive pen-in-mouth version remained inconclusive.

So not every famous effect was simply false. Some collapsed entirely, some shrank to a narrower and less exciting core, and the only way to tell which was large, preregistered, multi-lab testing.

concepts.title: What Survived, and What It Teaches
concepts.contentHtml:
The crisis did not find psychology empty. In Many Labs 1, ten of thirteen effects replicated consistently across 36 samples. Many Labs 2 replicated 15 of its 28 findings, and Camerer's team 13 of 21 high-profile experiments. Some areas did better still. In 2019 Christopher Soto's Life Outcomes of Personality Replication (LOOPR) project ran preregistered, high-powered replications (median N = 1,504) of 78 published links between the Big Five personality traits and consequential life outcomes. Overall, 87% of the replication attempts were statistically significant in the expected direction.1

Even the successes came with a discount. Soto's replication effects were typically 77% as strong as the originals.2 Camerer's group estimated that the true positives among their studies had a relative effect size of 71%, concluding that both false positives and inflated effect sizes of true positives contribute to imperfect reproducibility.3 This is lesson 1's winner's curse in action: when only significant results get noticed, even real effects arrive in the literature inflated. A replicated effect that comes back smaller is not a failure; it is the field correcting its estimate.

Across projects, the same features keep predicting survival. Soto found replicability was predicted by the effect size and design of the original study and by the sample size and power of the replication.4 The Reproducibility Project found that the strength of the original evidence mattered more than who ran the replication. The effects that failed tended to share a profile: small original samples, surprising claims, subtle manipulations of the social-priming kind, and analyses with room to move.

That gives you a practical rule for reading psychology now. Treat a single small study with a surprising result and p near .05 as a hypothesis. Give real weight to findings that have survived preregistered, well-powered, multi-site replication, and expect their true size to be smaller than the first report claimed.

title: Preregistration and Registered Reports
description: Fixing the plan, and the decision to publish, before the data arrive

concepts.title: Prediction Versus Postdiction
concepts.contentHtml:
In a 2018 paper titled "The preregistration revolution", Brian Nosek, Charles Ebersole, Alexander DeHaven and David Mellor set out the core distinction. Science needs postdiction, generating hypotheses from data already seen, and prediction, testing hypotheses against new data. Both are legitimate. Trouble starts when one is mistaken for the other, and ordinary hindsight bias, the I-knew-it-all-along effect, makes that mistake easy: once you have seen an outcome, it feels as though you predicted it.

Preregistration is the remedy. You define the research questions and analysis plan before observing the outcomes,1 and post the plan to an independent registry such as ClinicalTrials.gov or the Open Science Framework (OSF), which preserves it and makes it discoverable. A good preregistration fixes the hypotheses and primary outcomes, the sample size and stopping rule, the exclusion criteria and the statistical model. Then the selection of tests cannot be influenced by the data, and every test conducted is knowable.

Medicine moved first. US law requires clinical trials to be registered, and journals following the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors policy rarely publish trials that were not. Robert Kaplan and Veronica Irvin examined all 55 large trials funded by the US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute between 1970 and 2012 that tested drugs or dietary supplements for cardiovascular disease. Of 30 published before 2000, 17 (57%) showed a significant benefit on the primary outcome; of 25 published after 2000, only 2 (8%) did.2 After 2000, all of these trials had been registered prospectively in ClinicalTrials.gov; before 2000, none had.3

Preregistration does not ban exploration; it labels it. Unplanned analyses can still be reported, as exploratory, and deviations from the plan should be disclosed. What it rules out, in Nosek and colleagues' phrase, is dressing up discovery as tests of theoretical predictions.4

concepts.title: Registered Reports: Review Before Results
concepts.contentHtml:
Preregistration fixes the analysis but leaves the journal free to prefer positive results. Registered Reports remove that incentive too. Authors submit their introduction, hypotheses, methods and analysis plan before collecting data. Reviewers judge the question and the design, not the outcome. A protocol that survives this Stage 1 review receives an in-principle acceptance, which will not be revoked because of the results, only for failings such as not following the registered protocol. After the study is run, Stage 2 review checks that the authors did what they promised, and the paper is published whatever it found.

Chris Chambers of Cardiff University introduced the format at the journal Cortex in 2013.1 Over 300 journals now use Registered Reports, either as a regular submission option or in special issues.2 A sibling format, the Registered Replication Report, applied the same logic to multi-lab replications, including the ego-depletion and facial-feedback projects in lesson 5.

Does it change what gets published? In 2021 Anne Scheel, M. R. M. J. Schijen and Daniël Lakens of Eindhoven University of Technology compared all 71 psychology Registered Reports published by November 2018 with a random sample of 152 standard papers that said they tested a hypothesis. Analysing the first hypothesis in each, they found 96% positive results in standard reports but only 44% in Registered Reports.3 With direct replications excluded, the gap stayed nearly as large: 96% versus 50%. A literature in which 96% of tested hypotheses succeed is hard to believe; researchers are not that prescient.

The authors concluded that psychologists underreport negative results to an extent that threatens cumulative science,4 while noting that their study did not directly test whether Registered Reports reduce bias: the two literatures might also differ in how risky their hypotheses are. In a 2022 review, Chambers and Tzavella judged that Registered Reports are promoting reproducibility, transparency and self-correction, while acknowledging that they are not a universal solution for irreproducibility.5

concepts.title: Opening the Lab: Data, Badges and Big Teams
concepts.contentHtml:
Alongside preregistration came a push to make the rest of research visible. In November 2014 a committee of journal editors, funders and researchers met at the Center for Open Science in Charlottesville, Virginia, and drafted the Transparency and Openness Promotion (TOP) Guidelines, published in Science in 2015. There are eight modular standards:1 citation of data and code, replication, design transparency, research materials, data sharing, analytic methods (code), preregistration of studies and preregistration of analysis plans. Each comes in three levels, from simply stating whether materials are available up to requiring and checking them. By 15 June 2015 the signatories numbered 86 journals and 26 organisations.2

Some nudges were remarkably cheap. Beginning in January 2014, Psychological Science let authors earn open-practice badges, small icons on the article for open data or open materials. Before badges, less than 3% of its articles reported open data.3 After badges, 23% did, and 39% in the first half of 2015, with no change at comparison journals.4 Reporting openness did not guarantee it, but when badges were earned, the data were more likely to be actually available, correct, usable and complete.

The third shift was scale. Many findings rested on studies with insufficient power and unrepresentative samples, so researchers began pooling. The Psychological Science Accelerator, described in 2018, is a standing, decentralised network of laboratories that runs crowdsourced projects, novel studies or replications, in large and diverse samples.5 Many Labs, the Registered Replication Reports and the Many Smiles Collaboration belong to the same movement. Psychology was being rebuilt as a team activity: one preregistered protocol, dozens of labs, thousands of participants and data anyone can check.

title: Where the Reform Movement Stands
description: Threshold fights, retractions, the 2026 SCORE results and the problems still open

concepts.title: Arguing About Thresholds
concepts.contentHtml:
If p < .05 lets through too many false positives, why not move the line? In 2018 a group of 72 researchers,1 with Daniel Benjamin as first author and Brian Nosek, E. J. Wagenmakers and John Ioannidis among the co-authors, proposed in Nature Human Behaviour to change the default p-value threshold for statistical significance from 0.05 to 0.005 for claims of new discoveries.2 Their reasoning echoed lesson 1: a p-value just under .05 corresponds to weak evidence when expressed as a Bayes factor, and with realistic prior odds a large share of significant findings at that level are false.

A large group led by Daniël Lakens replied with "Justify your alpha". Rather than swap one universal threshold for another, they proposed that researchers should transparently report and justify all choices they make when designing a study, including the alpha level.3 A stricter threshold needs much larger samples for the same power, and it does nothing about flexible analysis or selective publication: a p-hacked .004 is no better than a p-hacked .04.

A third camp questions thresholds altogether. The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement noted that statisticians often supplement or even replace p-values with approaches that emphasise estimation over testing,4 such as confidence, credibility or prediction intervals, Bayesian methods, likelihood ratios and Bayes factors. On this view, the habit of sorting results into "significant" and "not significant" is itself part of the problem, because it feeds both the file drawer and the path-hunting that fills it.

The debate is unresolved, and its shape is instructive. Almost nobody now defends a lone p ≈ .04 from a small study as strong evidence. The disagreement is over the remedy: a stricter universal rule, flexible thresholds justified case by case, or a move away from yes-or-no verdicts towards effect sizes and their uncertainty.

concepts.title: Reform Under Scrutiny
concepts.contentHtml:
Reformers have not been immune to the problems they diagnosed, and how the field reacted when they slipped is part of the story. In November 2023 John Protzko, Jonathan Schooler, Brian Nosek, Leif Nelson and colleagues published a flagship study in Nature Human Behaviour. Four coordinated laboratories had made 16 new discoveries and then replicated one another's using rigour-enhancing practices: confirmatory tests, large samples, preregistration and methodological transparency. Replications succeeded 86% of the time, and effects replicated at 97% of their original size.1

Bak-Coleman and Devezer raised concerns, and in September 2024 the editors retracted the paper. The retraction notice cited misstatement of the hypotheses the meta-study was designed to test, lack of preregistration for measures and analyses supporting the titular claim2 despite statements in the article asserting preregistration, selection of outcome measures and analyses with knowledge of the data, and incomplete reporting. All authors agreed to the retraction because of incorrect statements of preregistration, but disagreed with the other concerns.3 A paper arguing that preregistration works had not itself been preregistered as claimed.

Fraud detection has also become more systematic. Uri Simonsohn, Joseph Simmons and Leif Nelson, the trio behind the false-positive paper of lesson 2, provided evidence questioning the validity of the data in a 2012 PNAS paper by Lisa Shu, Nina Mazar, Francesca Gino, Dan Ariely and Max Bazerman.4 That paper claimed that signing an honesty declaration at the top of a form, rather than the bottom, reduced cheating; its field experiment compared odometer mileage reported on 13,488 car-insurance policy forms.5 PNAS retracted it in 2021. Checks like this are only possible when data are available to people other than their authors, one reason open data became a central demand of the reform movement.

Neither episode shows that reform failed. Both show it working as designed: claims, including the reformers' own, were checked by outsiders with access to the materials, and corrected in public.

concepts.title: The 2026 Picture and the Problems Left
concepts.contentHtml:
The largest test so far appeared in Nature on 1 April 2026. SCORE (Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence), funded by the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) and coordinated by the Center for Open Science, began in 2019 and drew in 865 collaborators.1 Its replication study attempted 274 claims of positive results from 164 quantitative papers published from 2009 to 2018 in 54 journals across the social and behavioural sciences,2 including psychology, economics, political science, sociology, education and business. The replications were high powered, with a median of 99.6% power to detect the original effect sizes.

  • 151 of 274 claims (55.1%) replicated with significant results in the original pattern;3 weighted by paper, the rate was 49.3%.
  • The median effect size fell from r = 0.25 to r = 0.10, an 82.4% reduction in shared variance.
  • Replication rates varied only modestly across disciplines, from 42.5% to 63.1%.

So a decade after the Reproducibility Project, roughly half of published positive claims replicate, and the problem is not peculiar to psychology. SCORE also found that reproducibility (same data, same analysis), robustness (same data, different analysis) and replicability (new data) were only modestly correlated with one another. Reproducibility was higher in more recent publications and in journals that required data sharing, a hint that reforms pay off.4

Replication is necessary but not sufficient. Tal Yarkoni's generalizability crisis argument is that psychology's verbal hypotheses are routinely tested with statistical models that treat participants as a random sample but ignore the stimuli, tasks and research sites that researchers also intend to generalise over. That mismatch can dramatically inflate false-positive rates,5 and it licenses sweeping verbal claims the statistics never tested. A finding can replicate perfectly with the same stimuli and still not mean what its authors say. Beyond replication lie harder problems: theories that predict only "some effect", measures of uncertain validity and incentives that still prize novelty. Whether newly published, preregistered work replicates better than the 2009 to 2018 literature is the question the next generation of projects must answer.
